claims.claim: The nine-subunit lid includes the Zn2+-dependent deubiquitinase (DUB) Rpn11.
claims.source: The nine-subunit lid binds to one side of the base and thus further expands the regulatory particle's asymmetry contributed by the heterohexameric ATPase ring. The lid includes the Zn2+-dependent deubiquitinase (DUB) Rpn11 (Glickman et al., 1998b; Yao and Cohen, 2002; Verma et al., 2002) in a hetero-dimeric complex with another MPN-domain containing subunit, Rpn8 (Worden et al., 2014), as well as six scaffolding subunits, Rpn3, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 12.
claims.evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the proteasome lid, supported by citations to Glickman et al., 1998b; Yao and Cohen, 2002; Verma et al., 2002; and Worden et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The subunits Rpn5, Rpn6, and Rpn7 use their N-terminal TPR domains to specifically interact with the ATPase domains of Rpt4, Rpt3, and Rpt6, respectively.
claims.source: In addition to lid contacts with Rpn2 and the N-terminal regions of Rpt3 and Rpt6, the subunits Rpn5, Rpn6, and Rpn7 use their N-terminal TPR domains to specifically interact with the ATPase domains of Rpt4, Rpt3, and Rpt6, respectively (Lander et al., 2012; Lasker et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by citations to Lander et al., 2012 and Lasker et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Rpn5 and Rpn6 also contact the core peptidase and thus appear to form an external scaffold bridging the lid, base, and core subcomplexes within the proteasome holoenzyme.
claims.source: Rpn5 and Rpn6 also contact the core peptidase and thus appear to form an external scaffold bridging the lid, base, and core subcomplexes within the proteasome holoenzyme (Lander et al., 2012; Matyskiela et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by citations to Lander et al., 2012 and Matyskiela et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Previous cryo-electron microscopy studies identified multiple proteasome conformations with distinct relative orientations and contacts of base, lid, and core that are structurally conserved between yeast and human proteasomes.
claims.source: Previous cryo-electron microscopy studies identified multiple proteasome conformations with distinct relative orientations and contacts of base, lid, and core that are structurally conserved between yeast and human proteasomes (Matyskiela et al., 2013; Śledź et al., 2013; Unverdorben et al., 2014; Wehmer et al., 2017; Eisele et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2017; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In the absence of substrate, the proteasome exists in two conformations, s1 and s2, in which Rpt1-Rpt6 form a spiral staircase arrangement with Rpt3 in the top position.
claims.source: In the absence of substrate, the proteasome exists in two conformations, s1 and s2, in which Rpt1-Rpt6 form a spiral staircase arrangement with Rpt3 in the top position.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, as indicated by the context and citations in the surrounding text.

claims.claim: In the s1 state, the ATPase ring is not coaxially aligned with the core peptidase, and Rpn11 is offset from the central processing channel, allowing substrate access to the pore entrance.
claims.source: In the s1 state, the ATPase ring is not coaxially aligned with the core peptidase, and Rpn11 is offset from the central processing channel, allowing substrate access to the pore entrance.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, as indicated by the context and citations in the surrounding text.

claims.claim: The s2 state is characterized by a rotated lid position relative to the base and a coaxial alignment of Rpn11, the ATPase ring, and the core peptidase.
claims.source: In contrast, the s2 state is characterized by a rotated lid position relative to the base and a coaxial alignment of Rpn11, the ATPase ring, and the core peptidase (Unverdorben et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by citation to Unverdorben et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Substrate engagement induces conformations that are overall very similar to s2, with a continuous central channel for efficient substrate translocation and a centrally aligned Rpn11.
claims.source: Substrate engagement induces conformations that are overall very similar to s2, with a continuous central channel for efficient substrate translocation and a centrally aligned Rpn11 that leaves only a small gap to the subjacent Rpts for substrate to be pulled through, facilitating co-translocational deubiquitination (Matyskiela et al., 2013; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by citations to Matyskiela et al., 2013; de la Peña et al., 2018; and Dong et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The substrate-processing states, named s3-s6, show AAA+ motor conformations in which various Rpts adopt the individual vertical position in the spiral staircase, depending on the progression of the ATP-hydrolysis cycle in the hexamer.
claims.source: These substrate-processing states, named s3-s6 (Matyskiela et al., 2013; Unverdorben et al., 2014; Wehmer et al., 2017; Eisele et al., 2018; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019), show AAA+ motor conformations in which various Rpts adopt the individual vertical position in the spiral staircase, depending on the progression of the ATP-hydrolysis cycle in the hexamer.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The s5 state resembles s2, with the exception of the core gate that is open in s5 and closed in s2.
claims.source: The s5 state thereby resembles s2, with the exception of the core gate that is open in s5 and closed in s2 (Eisele et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by citation to Eisele et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Similar suites of substrate-engaged-like conformations can be induced by incubating the proteasome with non-hydrolyzable ATP analogs or introducing Walker-B mutations.
claims.source: Similar suites of substrate-engaged-like conformations can also be induced by incubating the proteasome with non-hydrolyzable ATP analogs (Śledź et al., 2013; Wehmer et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2017) or introducing Walker-B mutations (Eisele et al., 2018), both of which trap Rpts in the ATP-bound state and stabilize their interface to neighboring ATPase subunits in the hexamer.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by citations to Śledź et al., 2013; Wehmer et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2017; and Eisele et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Substrate engagement depends on the s1 state, in which the entrance to the central pore is accessible and the initiation region of a ubiquitin-receptor-bound substrate would be able to enter the AAA+ motor.
claims.source: Our recent studies on the coordination of proteasomal degradation steps suggested that substrate engagement depends on the s1 state, in which the entrance to the central pore is accessible and the initiation region of a ubiquitin-receptor-bound substrate would be able to enter the AAA+ motor (Bard et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior research from the authors' group, as indicated by citation to Bard et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Premature switching to substrate-processing states seemed to prevent substrate engagement, potentially due to Rpn11 obstructing the central pore.
claims.source: Premature switching to substrate-processing states seemed to prevent this substrate engagement, potentially due to Rpn11 obstructing the central pore.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior observations, representing speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Mutational studies with Walker-A or Walker-B substitutions in single ATPase subunits demonstrated the functional asymmetry of the proteasomal AAA+ motor.
claims.source: Mutational studies, in which nucleotide binding or hydrolysis of single ATPase subunits were disrupted by substitutions in the Walker-A or Walker-B motifs demonstrated the functional asymmetry of the proteasomal AAA+ motor, as the same mutations in different Rpts caused varied effects on cell viability and the degradation of ubiquitinated substrates (Eisele et al., 2018; Wendler et al., 2012; Rubin et al., 1998; Beckwith et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior mutational studies, supported by citations to Eisele et al., 2018; Wendler et al., 2012; Rubin et al., 1998; and Beckwith et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The contacts between Rpn5's TPR domain and the small AAA+ subdomain of Rpt3 are broken during the regulatory particle's transition from the substrate-free s1 state to any other state.
claims.source: Previous structural studies showed that the contacts between Rpn5's TPR domain and the small AAA+ subdomain of Rpt3 are broken during the regulatory particle's transition from the substrate-free s1 state to any other state (Matyskiela et al., 2013; Unverdorben et al., 2014; Wehmer et al., 2017; Eisele et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2017; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Loss of Rpn5-Rpt3 interactions perturbs the conformational landscape and allows the proteasome to more strongly populate substrate-engaged-like conformations even in the absence of substrate.
claims.source: Through mutations of the involved residues in Rpn5, we found that loss of these interactions perturbs the conformational landscape and allows the proteasome to more strongly populate substrate-engaged-like conformations even in the absence of substrate.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from negative-stain EM shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Walker-B mutations that prevent ATP hydrolysis in individual subunits of the AAA+ motor similarly disrupt the conformational equilibrium.
claims.source: Walker-B mutations that prevent ATP hydrolysis in individual subunits of the AAA+ motor similarly disrupt the conformational equilibrium.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from gate-opening assays, Ubp6 activity measurements, and degradation assays shown in Figures 3-5.

claims.claim: Perturbing the coordination between substrate-processing steps and conformational transitions of the proteasome's regulatory particle leads to decreased degradation rates, primarily by affecting the initiation of processing and shifting the rate-limiting step from substrate unfolding to engagement.
claims.source: In both cases, perturbing the coordination between substrate-processing steps and conformational transitions of the proteasome's regulatory particle leads to decreased degradation rates, primarily by affecting the initiation of processing and shifting the rate-limiting step from substrate unfolding to engagement.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from degradation assays, restart experiments, and substrate stability comparisons shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: The lid is required for proteasome function independent of deubiquitination.
claims.source: The lid is required for proteasome function independent of deubiquitination
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing that even with ubiquitin-independent substrate delivery, the lid is still required for efficient degradation, as shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Even though the dependence on Rpn11-mediated deubiquitination was eliminated using a ubiquitin-independent substrate-delivery system, presence of the lid was still required for efficient ATP-dependent degradation.
claims.source: Even though we eliminated the dependence on Rpn11-mediated deubiquitination, presence of the lid was still required for efficient ATP-dependent degradation (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: In contrast to other compartmental proteases, the proteasomal AAA+ motor and the 20S core peptidase together are not sufficient to catalyze ATP-dependent protein unfolding and degradation.
claims.source: In contrast to other compartmental proteases, the proteasomal AAA+ motor and the 20S core peptidase together are not sufficient to catalyze ATP-dependent protein unfolding and degradation.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing that base and core alone cannot efficiently degrade substrate without the lid, as shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Rpn5 uses a VTENKIF-sequence-containing loop to interact with the small AAA+ subdomain of the base subunit Rpt3 in the substrate-free s1 conformation, but not in any other conformation.
claims.source: The lid subunit Rpn5 (orange) uses a VTENKIF-sequence-containing loop (red) to interact with the small AAA+ subdomain of the base subunit Rpt3 in the substrate-free s1 conformation, but not in any other conformation, like s3 shown here (EMDB: 4321).
claims.evidence: This is established structural knowledge, supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1B and prior structural studies.

claims.claim: Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes show decreased rates for single-turnover degradation of ubiquitinated substrates compared to wild-type.
claims.source: Rates for the single-turnover degradation of a ubiquitinated, TAMRA-labeled G3P substrate with 54 amino acid tail derived from cyclin-b sequence (TAMRA-G3P) by wild-type and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes that were purified from S. cerevisiae (shaded) or in-vitro reconstituted using recombinant lid and base (solid) (N = 3, technical replicates, error bars plotted are SEM).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The Rpn5-VTENKIF mutation decreased the rate of both ubiquitin-dependent and ubiquitin-independent degradation.
claims.source: Mutating all residues in the Rpt3-contacting loop of Rpn5 (V125 - F131) to alanine (mutant denoted Rpn5-VTENKIF) decreased the rate of both, ubiquitin-dependent (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C) and ubiquitin-independent degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The loss of degradation activity in Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes is not primarily caused by defects in proteasome assembly.
claims.source: Importantly, this loss of degradation activity is not primarily caused by defects in proteasome assembly, which was found by native PAGE to be only slightly less efficient for the mutant compared to the wild-type enzyme (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from native PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Wild-type and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant lid have similar affinities for the base, as determined by the response of the base ATPase activity to lid binding during holoenzyme assembly.
claims.source: Furthermore, using the response of the base ATPase activity to lid binding during holoenzyme assembly, we determined similar affinities for wild-type and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant lid (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes show an elevated ATPase rate in the absence of substrate that increases in response to substrate processing, albeit to a lesser extent than for wild type.
claims.source: Despite their lower degradation activity, Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes show an elevated ATPase rate in the absence of substrate that increases in response to substrate processing, albeit to a lesser extent than for wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Proteasomes containing the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutation more strongly retained the Nas6 assembly chaperone during holoenzyme reconstitution.
claims.source: In agreement with recent findings (Nemec et al., 2019), proteasomes containing the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutation more strongly retained the Nas6 assembly chaperone during holoenzyme reconstitution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and consistent with prior findings cited from Nemec et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The presence of Nas6 is not the main cause for the observed decrease in degradation rate of Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes.
claims.source: However, this presence of Nas6 is not the main cause for the observed decrease in degradation rate, as purified endogenous proteasomes from S. cerevisiae carrying the same Rpn5 mutations also exhibit major deficiencies in single-turnover degradation reactions (Figure 1C), despite containing only negligible amounts of Nas6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data comparing reconstituted and endogenous proteasomes shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Substrate processing efficiently evicts most Nas6 from nascent Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that substrate processing efficiently evicts most Nas6 from nascent Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating that the initial Nas6 retention is not responsible for the steady-state substrate processing defect of the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The observed decrease in degradation activity of Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes appears to principally be caused by intrinsically compromised substrate processing, rather than defects in the assembly or composition of proteasome holoenzymes.
claims.source: Overall, the observed decrease in degradation activity appears to principally be caused by intrinsically compromised substrate processing, rather than the observed minor defects in the assembly or composition of proteasome holoenzymes (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations, representing an inference based on the data presented in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: ATP-bound wild-type proteasomes in the absence of substrate were observed in two conformations, s1 and s2.
claims.source: Consistent with previous observations, ATP-bound wild-type proteasomes in the absence of substrate were observed in two conformations, s1 and s2 (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Bard et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from negative-stain EM analysis, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, and consistent with prior observations cited from Bard et al., 2018a.

claims.claim: Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes showed only 37% of particles in the s1 state, while also populating substrate-engaged-like states (s3/s4/s6) that are absent from wild-type samples in the presence of ATP.
claims.source: In contrast to wild-type proteasomes with nearly equal distribution of s1 and s2 conformations, Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes showed only 37% of particles in the s1 state, while also populating substrate-engaged-like states (s3/s4/s6) that are absent from wild-type samples in the presence of ATP (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from negative-stain EM shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 5, and 6.

claims.claim: The Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant displayed predominantly s2 or s5 conformations, which are characterized by Rpn11 obstructing the central pore.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant displayed predominantly s2 or s5 conformations, which similar to s3, s4, and s6 are characterized by Rpn11 obstructing the central pore.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from negative-stain EM analysis.

claims.claim: The lower population of the s1 state in Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes resembles the scenario for Walker-B mutant proteasomes that were found to have perturbed conformational landscapes.
claims.source: The lower population of the s1 state resembles the scenario for Walker-B mutant proteasomes that in recent structural studies were found to have perturbed conformational landscapes as well (Eisele et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to prior findings, supported by citation to Eisele et al., 2018.

claims.claim: With bound ATPγS, the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes behaved similar to wild-type in shifting to a conformational distribution that is dominated by substrate engaged-like states.
claims.source: Importantly, however, with bound ATPγS the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes behaved similar to wild-type in shifting to a conformational distribution that is dominated by substrate engaged-like states, which demonstrates their retained ability to conformationally respond when Rpt subunits are trapped in an ATP-bound state.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from negative-stain EM analysis comparing ATP and ATPγS conditions.

claims.claim: Proteasome variants with a Walker-B mutation in Rpt1, Rpt2, Rpt3, or Rpt5 still maintain some Ubp6-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis.
claims.source: Despite significantly different basal ATPase rates, proteasome variants with a Walker-B mutation in Rpt1, Rpt2, Rpt3, or Rpt5 still maintain some Ubp6-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Rpt6-EQ and Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes did not respond to ubiquitin-bound Ubp6.
claims.source: However, two mutants with severe degradation defects, Rpt6-EQ and Rpt4-EQ, did not respond to ubiquitin-bound Ubp6 (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that a considerable fraction of those proteasomes adopt non-s1 states already in the absence of ubiquitin-bound Ubp6.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The failure of Rpt6-EQ and Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes to respond to ubiquitin-bound Ubp6 does not originate from compromised holoenzyme assembly.
claims.source: Additionally, this failure to respond to ubiquitin-bound Ubp6 does not originate from compromised holoenzyme assembly (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: All Walker-B mutants except Rpt1-EQ showed increased Ubp6 DUB activity in the presence ATP, but resembled the wild-type enzyme when in ATPγS.
claims.source: All Walker-B mutants except Rpt1-EQ showed increased Ubp6 DUB activity in the presence ATP, but resembled the wild-type enzyme when in ATPγS (Figure 3C), confirming their normal conformational response to nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Rpt6-EQ and Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes showing increased Ubp6 DUB activity in ATP is consistent with their lack of Ubp6-mediated ATPase stimulation and suggests that trapping Rpt4 or Rpt6 in permanent ATP-bound states populates non-s1 conformations, even in the absence of substrate or ATPγS.
claims.source: That Rpt6-EQ and Rpt4-EQ-mutant proteasomes show increased Ubp6 DUB activity in ATP is consistent with their lack of Ubp6-mediated ATPase stimulation and further suggests that trapping Rpt4 or Rpt6 in permanent ATP-bound states populates non-s1 conformations, even in the absence of substrate or ATPγS (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 3C, combining observations about ATPase stimulation and Ubp6 DUB activity.

claims.claim: The Rpt6-EQ mutant showed elevated gate opening in the presence of ATP that resembled the ATPγS-bound wild-type proteasome and did not further increase upon ATPγS addition.
claims.source: The Rpt6-EQ mutant showed elevated gate opening in the presence of ATP that resembled the ATPγS-bound wild-type proteasome and did not further increase upon ATPγS addition (Figure 3D), which is consistent with this variant being biased towards an engaged-like conformation due to trapping Rpt6 in a permanent ATP-bound state.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from gate-opening assays shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasome exhibited moderately increased core gate-opening and peptide-hydrolysis activity that still responded to ATPγS.
claims.source: Consistently, the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasome, whose conformational distribution appeared partially shifted in our EM analyses, exhibited moderately increased core gate-opening and peptide-hydrolysis activity that still responded to ATPγS.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from gate-opening assays.

claims.claim: Proteasomes containing the combined Rpn5-VTENKIF and Rpt6-EQ mutations behaved largely similar to the Rpt6-EQ mutant proteasome, indicating that preventing ATP hydrolysis in Rpt6 has a dominant effect on determining the conformational state.
claims.source: Proteasomes containing the combined Rpn5-VTENKIF and Rpt6-EQ mutations behaved largely similar to the Rpt6-EQ mutant proteasome, indicating that preventing ATP hydrolysis in Rpt6 and thus stabilizing the interface with Rpt3 has a dominant effect on determining the conformational state, at least with respect to core-particle docking and gate-opening.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from gate-opening assays comparing single and double mutants.

claims.claim: Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes' core-gate opening resembled the ATP-bound wild-type holoenzyme and was not responsive to ATPγS binding.
claims.source: Although Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes also appeared to be biased towards engaged-like, non-s1 conformations based on their crosstalk with Ubp6, their core-gate opening resembled the ATP-bound wild-type holoenzyme and was not responsive to ATPγS binding (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from gate-opening assays shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes displayed decreased assembly under non-equilibrium conditions in native-PAGE analyses.
claims.source: These proteasomes displayed decreased assembly under non-equilibrium conditions in native-PAGE analyses, which could explain some, yet not all of the gate-opening defects, as holoenzyme is clearly formed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from native-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The gate-opening activity of the Rpt4-EQ mutant was insensitive to increased base concentrations, arguing against an assembly defect as the main reason for the functional deficiencies.
claims.source: Moreover, the gate-opening activity of the Rpt4-EQ mutant was insensitive to increased base concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), arguing against an assembly defect as the main reason for the functional deficiencies and suggesting that a biased conformational landscape of assembled proteasome is largely responsible for the observed effects.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The Rpt4-EQ mutation seems to induce a partially distorted conformation that interacts with ubiquitin-bound Ubp6 similar to an engaged-state proteasome, but fails to properly dock with core particle for complete gate opening.
claims.source: The Rpt4-EQ mutation thus seems to induce a partially distorted conformation that interacts with ubiquitin-bound Ubp6 similar to an engaged-state proteasome, but fails to properly dock with core particle for complete gate opening.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple experimental observations about Rpt4-EQ mutant behavior.

claims.claim: Like the Rpt6-EQ mutation, the Rpt4-EQ mutation is dominant in determining the conformational state and therefore masks the stimulating gate-opening effects of the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutation in the combined mutant.
claims.source: Like the Rpt6-EQ mutation, the Rpt4-EQ mutation is dominant in determining the conformational state and therefore masks the stimulating gate-opening effects of the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutation in the combined mutant (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from gate-opening assays of double mutants shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Compromising the lid-base interface through Rpn5-VTENKIF mutations partially shifts the conformational equilibrium of the proteasome.
claims.source: Compromising the lid-base interface through Rpn5-VTENKIF mutations thus appears to partially shift the conformational equilibrium of the proteasome, while trapping Rpt6 or Rpt4 in ATP-bound states overrules those changes and further shifts the equilibrium towards either a fully engaged-like or a distorted, potentially off-pathway conformation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations, representing an inference based on the data.

claims.claim: Rpt6-EQ and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutations decreased the kcat for substrate degradation about 6-fold, with only minimal effects on Km.
claims.source: The Rpt6-EQ and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutations decreased the kcat for substrate degradation about 6-fold, with only minimal effects on Km (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from Michaelis-Menten kinetic analyses shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasome showed no discernable degradation activity at any substrate concentrations tested.
claims.source: Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasome showed no discernable degradation activity at any substrate concentrations tested (Figure 4A), and further measurements under single-turnover conditions revealed only a small change in anisotropy that we could attribute solely to substrate deubiquitination (Figure 4B), as no peptide products were detected in an end-point analysis by SDS-PAGE (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C.

claims.claim: Free Rpt4-EQ-containing regulatory particle harbored little deubiquitination activity compared to wild-type, Rpn5-VTENKIF, and Rpt6-EQ mutant RPs.
claims.source: Furthermore, free Rpt4-EQ-containing regulatory particle, a prominent species in the native-PAGE analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), harbored little deubiquitination activity compared to wild-type, Rpn5-VTENKIF, and Rpt6-EQ mutant RPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claims.claim: The deubiquitination activity of the Rpt4-EQ containing regulatory particle increases in a core-dependent manner.
claims.source: Interestingly, the deubiquitination activity of the Rpt4-EQ containing regulatory particle increases in a core-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that docking to the core particle positions Rpn11 in a more active conformation than in the free mutant RP (Dambacher et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and consistent with prior findings cited from Dambacher et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasome lacks substrate engagement or translocation activities, and thus appears degradation-incompetent.
claims.source: However, the Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasome lacks substrate engagement or translocation activities, and thus appears degradation-incompetent.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations about Rpt4-EQ mutant behavior.

claims.claim: The Rpt6-EQ and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutations do not considerably affect substrate engagement of proteasomes in the s1 state, based on the lack of major Km changes.
claims.source: Based on the lack of major Km changes, we can thus conclude that the Rpt6-EQ and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutations do not considerably affect substrate engagement of proteasomes in the s1 state (Bard et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from kinetic data, based on the relationship between Km and substrate engagement established in prior work cited from Bard et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Non-s1 states that are not yet substrate-engaged do not significantly contribute to substrate processing, because their coaxially aligned position of Rpn11 right above the entrance to the pore interferes with substrate-tail insertion for degradation.

results.result: The lid subcomplex is required for proteasome function independent of its deubiquitination activity. Using a ubiquitin-independent substrate-delivery system (SspB-fused base with ssrA-tagged substrates), the authors demonstrate that even when Rpn11-mediated deubiquitination is bypassed, the lid is still essential for efficient ATP-dependent degradation. This contrasts with other compartmental proteases where the AAA+ motor and peptidase alone are sufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 and C88 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and supplements. The ubiquitin-independent delivery system is a valid approach to isolate the lid's structural role from its deubiquitination function. The data clearly show that base + core alone cannot efficiently degrade substrate, while addition of lid restores activity. This is a key control demonstrating the lid's non-catalytic role.

results.result: The Rpn5-VTENKIF mutation, which disrupts the interaction between Rpn5's VTENKIF-containing loop and Rpt3's small AAA+ subdomain (a contact present only in the s1 state), significantly impairs proteasome degradation activity. The mutation decreases degradation rates for both ubiquitin-dependent and -independent substrates by approximately 6-fold, with minimal effects on proteasome assembly, lid-base affinity, or the presence of the Nas6 chaperone.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35-C44, C89, and C95 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence including degradation assays (Figure 1C), native PAGE (Figure 1—supplement 2), ATPase measurements (Figure 1—supplement 1D), and Nas6 retention studies (Figure 1—supplements 1E-F). The authors appropriately control for assembly defects and demonstrate that the degradation defect is intrinsic to substrate processing rather than holoenzyme formation. The structural basis (VTENKIF-Rpt3 contact) is well-established from prior cryo-EM studies.

results.result: Negative-stain EM analysis reveals that Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant proteasomes have a perturbed conformational landscape. In the presence of ATP, wild-type proteasomes show nearly equal distribution of s1 and s2 states, while Rpn5-VTENKIF mutants show only 37% s1 state and populate substrate-engaged-like states (s3/s4/s6) absent in wild-type. The mutant predominantly displays s2 or s5 conformations characterized by Rpn11 obstructing the central pore. With ATPγS, the mutant behaves similarly to wild-type, demonstrating retained conformational responsiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C45-C47, C49, and C91 are supported by negative-stain EM data (Figure 2 and supplements 3-6). The conformational classification is based on comparison to established atomic models from Eisele et al. 2018. While negative-stain EM has limited resolution compared to cryo-EM, the approach is appropriate for assessing conformational distributions. The observation that ATPγS normalizes the mutant's behavior provides important validation that the conformational machinery remains intact.

results.result: Walker-B mutations in individual Rpt subunits differentially affect proteasome conformational equilibrium. Rpt6-EQ and Rpt4-EQ mutants show severe degradation defects and do not respond to ubiquitin-bound Ubp6 in ATPase stimulation assays, suggesting they adopt non-s1 states even without substrate. Rpt6-EQ shows elevated gate opening in ATP that resembles ATPγS-bound wild-type and does not further increase with ATPγS. Other Walker-B mutants (Rpt1, Rpt2, Rpt3, Rpt5) retain some Ubp6-mediated ATPase stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C30, C50-C55, C103, and C108 are well-supported by functional assays including Ubp6-mediated ATPase stimulation (Figure 3B), Ubp6 DUB activity (Figure 3C), and gate-opening measurements (Figure 3D). The use of Ubp6 as a conformational reporter is validated by prior work. The differential effects of Walker-B mutations in different Rpt subunits are consistent with the functional asymmetry of the AAA+ motor. Assembly controls (Figure 1—supplement 2, Figure 3—supplement 2) appropriately rule out assembly defects as the primary cause.

results.result: Disrupting Rpn5-base or Rpt6 nucleotide state primarily affects degradation initiation rather than later processing steps. Michaelis-Menten analysis shows Rpt6-EQ and Rpn5-VTENKIF mutations decrease kcat ~6-fold with minimal Km effects, indicating substrate engagement in the s1 state is not impaired. Restart experiments after o-PA-induced stalling demonstrate that both mutants fully regain wild-type degradation rates, confirming that only tail insertion and engagement are compromised while subsequent deubiquitination, unfolding, and translocation remain intact.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C31, C64, C69, C78-C80, and C86 are strongly supported by kinetic analyses (Figure 4A), restart experiments (Figure 5B), and FRET-based tail insertion assays (Figure 5A, supplements). The restart experiment is particularly compelling evidence that later steps are unaffected. The interpretation that minimal Km changes indicate normal engagement in s1 state is reasonable given prior work establishing the relationship between Km and engagement (Bard et al. 2019). The shift in rate-limiting step from unfolding to engagement is a logical inference from the data.

results.result: FRET-based tail insertion assays show that substrate tail insertion takes approximately twice as long for Rpn5-VTENKIF and Rpt6-EQ mutant proteasomes compared to wild-type. Minimal tail insertion is observed with ATPγS or in the absence of core and lid for both wild-type and mutant proteasomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by FRET measurements (Figure 5A, Figure 5—supplement 1). The FRET assay using Cy3-labeled proteasomes and Cy5-labeled substrate with o-PA-inhibited Rpn11 is well-designed to specifically measure tail insertion. The ~2-fold increase in insertion time for mutants is consistent with their conformational defects. Controls with ATPγS and incomplete proteasomes validate the assay specificity.

results.result: Rpn5-VTENKIF and Rpt6-EQ mutant proteasomes fully regain wild-type degradation rates when restarted after an o-PA-induced deubiquitination stall, demonstrating that post-engagement processing steps (deubiquitination, unfolding, translocation) are not compromised by these mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C77 and C107 are strongly supported by restart experiment data (Figure 5B, Figure 5—supplement 2A). The experimental design is elegant: by stalling proteasomes after engagement but before deubiquitination, then restarting with Zn2+, the authors isolate post-engagement steps. The complete rescue of degradation rates in mutants is compelling evidence that only initiation is affected. This is a critical result distinguishing engagement defects from processing defects.

results.result: Substrate stability comparison experiments reveal that the rate-limiting step differs between wild-type and mutant proteasomes depending on substrate stability. Wild-type degrades destabilized titin-I27V13P/V15P significantly faster than non-destabilized titin-I27, while Rpn5-VTENKIF and Rpt6-EQ mutants show minimal differences. All three proteasome variants degrade non-destabilized titin-I27 at comparable rates, indicating that for highly stable substrates, unfolding becomes rate-limiting even for mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are supported by degradation rate measurements with substrates of varying stability (Figure 5C, Figure 5—supplement 2B). The interpretation that unfolding is not rate-limiting for mutants with destabilized substrates is logical given the similar rates for substrates with different stabilities. The convergence of rates for the stable substrate suggests unfolding becomes limiting for all variants. This provides additional evidence that engagement, not unfolding, is the primary defect in mutants.

results.result: Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes are degradation-incompetent, showing no discernible degradation activity at any substrate concentration tested. Single-turnover measurements reveal only deubiquitination without peptide product formation. Free Rpt4-EQ regulatory particle shows minimal deubiquitination activity that increases upon core docking, but the holoenzyme still lacks substrate engagement or translocation activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 and C105 are well-supported by Michaelis-Menten analysis (Figure 4A), single-turnover measurements (Figure 4B-C), and regulatory particle deubiquitination assays (Figure 4—supplement 1). The complete loss of degradation activity despite retained deubiquitination and assembly is striking. The authors appropriately distinguish between deubiquitination and degradation. This explains the lethality of this mutant in yeast (Eisele et al. 2018) and highlights Rpt4's critical role.

results.result: Rpt4-EQ mutant proteasomes display unusual behavior: they interact with ubiquitin-bound Ubp6 similar to engaged-state proteasomes but fail to properly open the core gate. Gate-opening resembles ATP-bound wild-type and is unresponsive to ATPγS. While native-PAGE shows decreased assembly under non-equilibrium conditions, the gate-opening defect persists at increased base concentrations, suggesting a biased conformational landscape rather than assembly defects. The Rpt4-EQ mutation is dominant over Rpn5-VTENKIF in determining conformational state.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by gate-opening assays (Figure 3D), native-PAGE (Figure 1—supplement 2), and concentration-dependence studies (Figure 3—supplement 2). The interpretation that Rpt4-EQ induces a partially distorted conformation is reasonable given the discordant Ubp6 and gate-opening behaviors. The dominance experiments with double mutants provide additional mechanistic insight. However, the exact nature of the Rpt4-EQ conformational defect remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: Rpn5-VTENKIF mutation shows moderately increased core gate-opening that still responds to ATPγS, indicating partial conformational shift. Double mutant analysis reveals that Rpt6-EQ and Rpt4-EQ mutations are dominant over Rpn5-VTENKIF for gate-opening, suggesting nucleotide states in the motor primarily drive conformational switching. However, Rpn5-VTENKIF dominates degradation defects when combined with Rpt6-EQ, potentially due to different dynamics of conformational switching.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C63, C109-C110 are supported by gate-opening assays with single and double mutants (Figure 3D). The epistasis analysis provides insight into the relative contributions of lid-base contacts versus motor nucleotide states. The interpretation that different dynamics explain the discordant dominance patterns is speculative but reasonable. These results help establish a hierarchy of conformational control mechanisms.

results.result: The study establishes that Rpn5-VTENKIF and Rpt6-EQ mutations affect conformational switching through distinct mechanisms despite producing similar degradation defects. Rpn5-VTENKIF disrupts critical lid-base interactions and destabilizes the s1 state through spontaneous re-equilibration. Rpt6-EQ stabilizes substrate-processing states and inhibits sequential ATPase cycle progression, pulling equilibrium away from s1. Both highlight the critical importance of s1 state population for substrate-tail insertion and engagement before conformational switching to processing states.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94, C112-C115 represent the major mechanistic conclusions of the study, synthesizing data from multiple experimental approaches. The distinction between destabilizing s1 (Rpn5-VTENKIF) versus stabilizing processing states (Rpt6-EQ) is well-supported by the conformational, kinetic, and functional data. The proposal that lid-base contact breaking is an early step in s1→processing transition (C93-C94) is a reasonable mechanistic hypothesis based on structural observations, though somewhat speculative.

results.result: The authors propose that non-s1 states do not significantly contribute to substrate processing because Rpn11's coaxially aligned position obstructs substrate-tail insertion and limits DUB access. They hypothesize that weakening lid-base interactions may increase conformational switching dynamics and shorten s1 state lifetime below the time constant for tail insertion (~1.6 s), which would disrupt the kinetic-gateway substrate-selection mechanism and cause degradation defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72, C98-C100 represent mechanistic hypotheses and speculation rather than directly demonstrated results. While the structural reasoning about Rpn11 obstruction is sound and supported by prior work, the proposal about shortened s1 lifetime and increased dynamics is not directly tested. The EM provides static snapshots of conformational distributions but cannot measure dynamics or state lifetimes. The hypothesis is plausible and consistent with the data, but would require additional experiments (e.g., single-molecule studies) to validate.

results.result: The authors speculate that the alternative mechanisms for shifting conformational landscape (lid-base contacts vs. motor nucleotide states) suggest numerous possibilities for regulatory fine-tuning through posttranslational modifications or binding partners. They propose that modulating conformational equilibria could differentially influence turnover of specific substrate pools, and expect this regulatory mechanism to be conserved in eukaryotic proteasomes given structural/functional conservation between yeast and humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 represent speculation about broader implications rather than demonstrated results. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by existing knowledge of proteasome regulation (VerPlank citations), these are hypotheses for future work rather than conclusions from the current study. The observation that mutations affect different substrates differently (C118) provides some support, but the regulatory implications remain to be tested. Conservation (C119) is a reasonable expectation but not demonstrated here.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on proteasome structure, function, and conformational states, establishing the context for the current work. This includes the proteasome's role in proteostasis, its structural organization (core, base, lid), the AAA+ motor mechanism, substrate requirements, conformational states (s1-s6) identified by prior cryo-EM studies, and the functional asymmetry of Rpt subunits demonstrated by mutational studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C6-C28, and C87 represent established knowledge from prior work, appropriately cited throughout. These provide essential context but are not novel findings of this study. The authors accurately represent prior work and cite appropriate references. This background is necessary to understand the significance of the current findings but does not constitute a result of this manuscript.

results.result: The study compares Rpn5-VTENKIF effects to prior Walker-B mutant studies and provides structural context for Rpt6 and Rpt4 nucleotide states in different conformations. The comparison reveals similarities in conformational landscape perturbations while noting unique features of each mutant. The authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether Rpt4-EQ defects originate solely from conformational bias or also affect other degradation steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C90, C92, C101-C102, C104, C106, and C111 represent comparisons to prior work and acknowledgment of limitations. The comparison to Eisele et al. 2018 is appropriate and helps contextualize the findings. The structural information about Rpt6 nucleotide states (C101-C102) is established knowledge used to interpret results. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about Rpt4-EQ mechanism (C106) is appropriate scientific caution. These are valid interpretive points but not primary results.

results.result: The authors note that their prior work established that substrate engagement triggers the conformational change from s1, breaking Rpn5-VTENKIF contacts. They emphasize that the Rpn5-VTENKIF mutant contains an unmodified ATPase ring with mutations relevant only in s1 state, providing cleaner evidence for s1-state requirement than prior ATPγS experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C73, C96-C97 represent methodological context and comparison to prior approaches. The point that Rpn5-VTENKIF provides cleaner evidence than ATPγS experiments (C97) is valid and represents an important advance in experimental design. However, this is more about the strength of the approach than a novel result per se. The reference to prior work (C73) provides necessary context.
